2. Data Preprocessing¶

  • Missing values: none were found, so nothing needs to be imputed.
  • Feature selection: as required, only Annual Income (k$) and Spending Score (1-100) are used.
  • Scaling: K-Means is distance-based, so features on larger scales dominate the distance. StandardScaler (mean 0, std 1) puts both features on an equal footing.
In [4]:
features = ["Annual Income (k$)", "Spending Score (1-100)"]
X = mall[features]

# Quick look at the two selected features
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))
sns.histplot(X[features[0]], kde=True, ax=axes[0], color="#1d7a8c")
sns.histplot(X[features[1]], kde=True, ax=axes[1], color="#d1495b")
axes[2].scatter(X[features[0]], X[features[1]], alpha=0.7, color="gray")
axes[0].set_title("Annual income distribution"); axes[1].set_title("Spending score distribution")
axes[2].set(title="Raw data (no labels yet)", xlabel=features[0], ylabel=features[1])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# Feature scaling
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)
print("Scaled means:", X_scaled.mean(axis=0).round(3), "| scaled std:", X_scaled.std(axis=0).round(3))

Scaled means: [-0. -0.] | scaled std: [1. 1.]

3. Elbow Method – Choosing the Optimal k¶

The inertia (within-cluster sum of squared distances) always falls as k grows. The elbow is the k after which adding clusters gives only small gains. To back up the visual choice, two extra checks are shown: the silhouette score (higher = better separated clusters) and the point that lies farthest from the straight line joining the first and last inertia values (a simple automatic elbow detector).

In [5]:
k_range = range(1, 11)
inertia, silhouette = [], {}
for k in k_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_scaled)
    inertia.append(km.inertia_)
    if k > 1:
        silhouette[k] = silhouette_score(X_scaled, km.labels_)

# Elbow detector: distance of each (k, inertia) point from the chord joining the first and last point
ks = np.array(list(k_range))
(x1, y1), (x2, y2) = (ks[0], inertia[0]), (ks[-1], inertia[-1])
dist = [abs((x2 - x1) * (y1 - y) - (x1 - x) * (y2 - y1)) / np.hypot(x2 - x1, y2 - y1) for x, y in zip(ks, inertia)]
optimal_k = int(ks[int(np.argmax(dist))])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.5))
axes[0].plot(ks, inertia, marker="o", color="#1d3557")
axes[0].axvline(optimal_k, color="#d1495b", ls="--", label=f"elbow at k = {optimal_k}")
axes[0].set(title="Elbow Method", xlabel="Number of clusters (k)", ylabel="Inertia (WCSS)", xticks=ks)
axes[0].legend()
axes[1].plot(list(silhouette), list(silhouette.values()), marker="o", color="#2a9d8f")
axes[1].axvline(optimal_k, color="#d1495b", ls="--")
axes[1].set(title="Silhouette score", xlabel="Number of clusters (k)", ylabel="Silhouette", xticks=ks[1:])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Inertia by k:", {int(k): round(v, 1) for k, v in zip(ks, inertia)})
print("Silhouette by k:", {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in silhouette.items()})
print(f"\nOptimal number of clusters chosen: k = {optimal_k}")

Inertia by k: {1: 400.0, 2: 269.7, 3: 157.7, 4: 108.9, 5: 65.6, 6: 55.1, 7: 44.9, 8: 37.2, 9: 32.4, 10: 30.0}
Silhouette by k: {2: 0.321, 3: 0.467, 4: 0.494, 5: 0.555, 6: 0.54, 7: 0.528, 8: 0.455, 9: 0.457, 10: 0.443}

Optimal number of clusters chosen: k = 5

4. Train the Final K-Means Model and Report the Inertia¶

In [6]:
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=optimal_k, n_init=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
mall["Cluster"] = kmeans.fit_predict(X_scaled)

# Centroids back in the original units (k$ and score) so they can be read directly
centroids = scaler.inverse_transform(kmeans.cluster_centers_)

# Inertia in original units, for interpretation (sum of squared distances to the own centroid)
inertia_original = ((X.values - centroids[mall["Cluster"]]) ** 2).sum()

print(f"Final model inertia (scaled features):   {kmeans.inertia_:.3f}")
print(f"Same inertia in original units:          {inertia_original:,.1f}")
print(f"Silhouette score of the final clustering: {silhouette_score(X_scaled, kmeans.labels_):.3f}")

Final model inertia (scaled features):   65.568
Same inertia in original units:          44,448.5
Silhouette score of the final clustering: 0.555

5. Visualise the Clusters¶

In [7]:
# Name each cluster from where its centroid lies (z-score > 0 = above average)
def persona(z_income, z_spend):
    if abs(z_income) < 0.5 and abs(z_spend) < 0.5:
        return "Average income, average spending"
    return {(True, True): "High income, high spending",
            (True, False): "High income, low spending",
            (False, True): "Low income, high spending",
            (False, False): "Low income, low spending"}[(z_income > 0, z_spend > 0)]

names = {c: persona(*kmeans.cluster_centers_[c]) for c in range(optimal_k)}
palette = sns.color_palette("Set1", optimal_k)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 6))
for c in range(optimal_k):
    pts = mall[mall["Cluster"] == c]
    plt.scatter(pts[features[0]], pts[features[1]], s=60, color=palette[c], alpha=0.8,
                label=f"Cluster {c}: {names[c]} (n={len(pts)})")
plt.scatter(centroids[:, 0], centroids[:, 1], s=350, c="black", marker="*", label="Centroids")
plt.title(f"Mall customer segments (K-Means, k = {optimal_k})")
plt.xlabel("Annual Income (k$)"); plt.ylabel("Spending Score (1-100)")
plt.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 0.5))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

7. Findings and Insights¶

  • k = 5 is the right number of clusters. The inertia curve bends sharply at k = 5 (inertia 65.6) and improves only slowly afterwards; the automatic elbow detector also picks 5, and the silhouette score peaks at k = 5 (0.555).
  • Final model inertia = 65.57 on the scaled features (≈ 44,448 in original k$/score units); the silhouette of 0.555 indicates well-separated, compact clusters.
  • Five meaningful customer segments:
Segment Customers Avg. income (k$) Avg. spending score Avg. age Suggested action
High income, high spending 39 86.5 82.1 32.7 Primary target – premium offers, loyalty programmes
Low income, high spending 22 25.7 79.4 25.3 Young, enthusiastic – trendy / discount offers
Average income, average spending 81 55.3 49.5 42.7 Largest group – steady, mainstream promotions
High income, low spending 35 88.2 17.1 41.1 Under-served – personalised campaigns to unlock spending
Low income, low spending 23 26.3 20.9 45.2 Price-sensitive – low marketing priority
  • Income alone does not predict spending: customers with similar high incomes split into big spenders (86.5 k$, score 82) and very frugal ones (88.2 k$, score 17) – exactly why a two-feature clustering is more useful than income bands.
  • The two high-spending groups are the youngest (average age 25 and 33), the low-spending groups the oldest (41–45).
  • Limitation: K-Means assumes roughly round clusters and needs k in advance; here the data are visibly compact blobs, so it works very well.

# Exploratory plot: which measurements separate the species?
sns.pairplot(iris, hue="Species", palette="Set1", height=2.2, plot_kws={"alpha": 0.8})

The pair plot shows setosa is completely separated from the other two species (especially by petal length / width), while versicolor and virginica overlap slightly – that overlap is where any classification errors will come from.

2. Data Preprocessing and Train/Test Split¶

  • Missing values: none.
  • Split: 80 % training / 20 % testing, stratified so each species keeps the same share in both sets.
  • Scaling: KNN is distance-based, so features are standardised. The scaler is fitted on the training data only and then applied to the test data, so no test information leaks into training.
In [11]:
X_iris = iris.drop(columns="Species")
y_iris = iris["Species"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_iris, y_iris, test_size=0.20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, stratify=y_iris
)
print("Training samples:", len(X_train), "| Testing samples:", len(X_test))
print("Test class counts:", y_test.value_counts().to_dict())

iris_scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_train)             # learn mean / std from training data only
X_train_s = iris_scaler.transform(X_train)
X_test_s = iris_scaler.transform(X_test)

Training samples: 120 | Testing samples: 30
Test class counts: {'Iris-setosa': 10, 'Iris-virginica': 10, 'Iris-versicolor': 10}

y_pred = knn.predict(X_test_s)

5. Findings and Insights¶

  • The default KNN reaches 93.3 % accuracy (28 of 30 test flowers) with macro precision 0.944, recall 0.933 and F1 0.933.
  • Setosa is classified perfectly (precision and recall 1.00) and every versicolor is found (recall 1.00). The only errors are 2 virginica flowers predicted as versicolor (virginica recall 0.80, versicolor precision 0.83) – the two species whose measurements overlap in the pair plot.
  • With only 30 test flowers, one mistake = 3.3 percentage points of accuracy, so small differences between models on this test set should be interpreted cautiously (cross-validation in Task 2(a) gives a steadier estimate).
  • KNN needs scaling (done) and has no training phase – it stores the data and votes among the k nearest neighbours, so the choice of k and the weighting matter; these are tuned next.

Task 1(c) – Naive Bayes Classification: SMS Spam Detection¶

Goal: classify an SMS as ham (legitimate) or spam. The classes are imbalanced, so accuracy alone is misleading – the key metrics are the precision and recall of the spam class:

  • Precision (spam) – of the messages flagged as spam, how many really are (low precision = legitimate messages get blocked).
  • Recall (spam) – of all real spam, how much is caught (low recall = spam reaches the inbox).

1. Load the Dataset and Inspect It¶

In [15]:

Handling duplicates. 403 messages appear more than once. If the same text lands in both the training and the test set, the test score is inflated (the model has "seen the answer"), so exact duplicates are removed before splitting.

In [16]:
sms = sms.drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)
counts = sms["label"].value_counts()
print("After removing duplicates:", sms.shape[0], "messages")

for i, n in enumerate(counts.values):
    axes[0].text(i, n + 40, f"{n} ({n / len(sms):.1%})", ha="center", fontweight="bold")
axes[0].set(title="Class distribution (imbalanced)", ylabel="messages")

sms["length"] = sms["text"].str.len()
sns.histplot(data=sms, x="length", hue="label", palette={"ham": "#2a9d8f", "spam": "#d1495b"},
             bins=40, stat="density", common_norm=False, alpha=0.5, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set(title="Message length (characters)")

def top_words(label, n=10):
    vec = CountVectorizer(stop_words="english")
    counts_ = vec.fit_transform(sms.loc[sms["label"] == label, "text"]).sum(axis=0).A1
    return pd.Series(counts_, index=vec.get_feature_names_out()).nlargest(n).sort_values()
spam_words = top_words("spam")
axes[2].barh(spam_words.index, spam_words.values, color="#d1495b")
axes[2].set(title="Top 10 words in spam messages")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("Average length:", sms.groupby("label")["length"].mean().round(0).to_dict())
print("Top ham words :", list(top_words("ham").index[::-1]))

After removing duplicates: 5169 messages
ham: 4516 (87.4%)   spam: 653 (12.6%)

Average length: {'ham': 71.0, 'spam': 138.0}
Top ham words : ['gt', 'lt', 'just', 'ok', 'll', 'got', 'know', 'like', 'good', 'come']

EDA insight: spam messages are about twice as long (138 vs. 71 characters on average) and are full of call-to-action words – free, txt, stop, mobile, claim, reply, prize. Ham messages use everyday conversational words (ok, just, got, know, good, come). This vocabulary difference is exactly what Naive Bayes exploits.

2. Data Preprocessing and Train/Test Split¶

  • Label encoding: ham → 0, spam → 1.
  • Text → numbers: CountVectorizer turns each message into word counts (a bag of words). The vectoriser is part of a Pipeline, so it is fitted on training messages only.
  • Split: 80 / 20, stratified so both sets keep ≈ 12.6 % spam.
  • Model choice: MultinomialNB is the natural Naive Bayes for word counts. GaussianNB assumes continuous, bell-shaped features and is not suited to sparse count data.
In [17]:
y_sms = (sms["label"] == "spam").astype(int)            # ham = 0, spam = 1
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
    sms["text"], y_sms, test_size=0.20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, stratify=y_sms
)
print(f"Training messages: {len(X_tr)} (spam {y_tr.mean():.1%})  |  Testing messages: {len(X_te)} (spam {y_te.mean():.1%}, {int(y_te.sum())} spam)")

Training messages: 4135 (spam 12.6%)  |  Testing messages: 1034 (spam 12.7%, 131 spam)

3. Baseline Model: CountVectorizer + MultinomialNB¶

In [18]:
def spam_scores(y_true, y_pred):
    """Metrics that matter for an imbalanced problem (spam = positive class)."""
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)
    return {"Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred),
            "Spam precision": precision_score(y_true, y_pred),
            "Spam recall": recall_score(y_true, y_pred),
            "Spam F1": f1_score(y_true, y_pred),
            "Missed spam (FN)": int(cm[1, 0]),
            "Ham blocked (FP)": int(cm[0, 1])}


baseline = Pipeline([("vec", CountVectorizer()), ("nb", MultinomialNB())])
baseline.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
y_pred_base = baseline.predict(X_te)

print("Classification report – baseline:\n")
print(classification_report(y_te, y_pred_base, target_names=["ham", "spam"], digits=3))
print("Confusion matrix (rows = actual, columns = predicted):")
print(confusion_matrix(y_te, y_pred_base))

ax.set_title("Baseline Naive Bayes – confusion matrix"); ax.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Baseline reading: accuracy looks excellent (98.3 %), but this is partly because 87 % of messages are ham. The spam-specific scores tell the real story: precision 0.959 but recall only 0.901 – 13 of the 131 spam messages reach the inbox – and 5 legitimate messages are wrongly blocked.

4. Improving the Scores for the Imbalanced Dataset¶

Several standard techniques are compared. Each is trained on the training set only and evaluated on the same untouched test set:

Code Technique Idea
A Baseline CountVectorizer + MultinomialNB (α = 1, class prior learned from the data)
B TF-IDF features down-weights very common words
C Uniform class prior (fit_prior=False) stops the model from favouring the majority class 'ham' by default
D Random over-sampling of spam duplicate spam messages in the training set only until both classes are equal
E ComplementNB Naive Bayes variant designed for imbalanced text
F GridSearchCV over vectoriser, n-grams, stop-words, α and prior tuned for the F1-score of the spam class (5-fold CV on training data)
G F + decision-threshold tuning threshold chosen from cross-validated (out-of-fold) training predictions to maximise spam F1
In [20]:
results = {}
results["A  Baseline (Count + MNB)"] = spam_scores(y_te, y_pred_base)

# B - TF-IDF features
tfidf = Pipeline([("vec", TfidfVectorizer()), ("nb", MultinomialNB())]).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
results["B  TF-IDF + MNB"] = spam_scores(y_te, tfidf.predict(X_te))

# C - uniform class prior
uniform = Pipeline([("vec", CountVectorizer()), ("nb", MultinomialNB(fit_prior=False))]).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
results["C  Uniform class prior"] = spam_scores(y_te, uniform.predict(X_te))

# D - random over-sampling of the minority class (training data only!)
train_df = pd.DataFrame({"text": X_tr, "y": y_tr})
ham_train, spam_train = train_df[train_df["y"] == 0], train_df[train_df["y"] == 1]
oversampled = pd.concat([ham_train, spam_train.sample(len(ham_train), replace=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)])
print(f"Training set after over-sampling: ham = {(oversampled['y'] == 0).sum()}, spam = {(oversampled['y'] == 1).sum()}")
over = Pipeline([("vec", CountVectorizer()), ("nb", MultinomialNB())]).fit(oversampled["text"], oversampled["y"])
results["D  Over-sampled spam"] = spam_scores(y_te, over.predict(X_te))

# E - Complement Naive Bayes
comp = Pipeline([("vec", CountVectorizer()), ("nb", ComplementNB())]).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
results["E  ComplementNB"] = spam_scores(y_te, comp.predict(X_te))

Training set after over-sampling: ham = 3613, spam = 3613

# F - GridSearchCV: vectoriser type, n-grams, min_df, stop-words, smoothing alpha and class prior
cv5 = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
param_grid = {
    "vec": [CountVectorizer(), TfidfVectorizer()],
    "vec__ngram_range": [(1, 1), (1, 2)],
    "vec__min_df": [1, 2],
    "vec__stop_words": [None, "english"],
    "nb__alpha": [0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0],
    "nb__fit_prior": [True, False],
}

                      param_grid, cv=cv5, scoring="f1", n_jobs=1)
search.fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print("Combinations searched:", len(search.cv_results_["params"]))
print("Best parameters:", {k: (type(v).__name__ if k == "vec" else v) for k, v in search.best_params_.items()})
print(f"Best cross-validated spam F1: {search.best_score_:.4f}")

Combinations searched: 128
Best parameters: {'nb__alpha': 0.1, 'nb__fit_prior': True, 'vec': 'CountVectorizer', 'vec__min_df': 1, 'vec__ngram_range': (1, 1), 'vec__stop_words': None}

In [22]:
# G - decision-threshold tuning, chosen on OUT-OF-FOLD training probabilities (the test set is not touched)
best_model = search.best_estimator_
oof_proba = cross_val_predict(best_model, X_tr, y_tr, cv=cv5, method="predict_proba")[:, 1]
thresholds = np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 91)
oof_f1 = [f1_score(y_tr, oof_proba >= t) for t in thresholds]
best_t = float(thresholds[int(np.argmax(oof_f1))])
print(f"Best threshold on out-of-fold predictions: {best_t:.2f}  (spam F1 = {max(oof_f1):.4f}; default threshold is 0.50)")

proba_te = best_model.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
y_pred_final = (proba_te >= best_t).astype(int)
results["G  Tuned + threshold"] = spam_scores(y_te, y_pred_final)

summary = pd.DataFrame(results).T.astype({"Missed spam (FN)": int, "Ham blocked (FP)": int})
display(summary.round(4))

6. Findings and Insights¶

  • Accuracy is misleading here. Every technique scores 95–99 % accuracy because 87 % of messages are ham; the precision / recall of the spam class separate the models.
  • There is a precision–recall trade-off. Techniques that tell the model to take spam more seriously – uniform prior (C), over-sampling (D) and ComplementNB (E) – raise spam recall from 0.901 to 0.94–0.95 (missed spam falls from 13 to 6–8) but precision drops from 0.959 to ≈ 0.87 (18–19 legitimate messages blocked instead of 5). Over-sampling and the uniform prior behave almost identically because both remove the model's built-in preference for 'ham'.
  • TF-IDF with default smoothing (B) hurts recall (0.626, 49 missed spam) – a reminder that Naive Bayes hyper-parameters (especially the smoothing α) must be tuned together with the feature extraction.
  • GridSearchCV (F) chose plain word counts, unigrams, no stop-word removal, α = 0.1 and the learned prior; it gives a better-balanced model (precision 0.925, recall 0.939, F1 0.932 vs. 0.929 baseline).
  • Threshold tuning (G) gives the best overall result: spam precision 0.983, recall 0.901 and F1 0.940 (the highest), with only 2 legitimate messages blocked instead of 5 and the same 13 missed spam as the baseline. The threshold (0.85) was chosen from cross-validated predictions on the training data, so the test score is an honest estimate.
  • Which model to use? For a real SMS filter, blocking a legitimate message is usually worse than letting some spam through, so G (precision-focused) is the best choice; if missing spam is the bigger concern, C/E (recall 0.954) is the alternative. The trade-off is a business decision, not a modelling one.
  • Limitation: the test set has only 131 spam messages, so one message changes recall by 0.8 points – differences of 1–2 messages between the tuned variants are within noise.

Task 2(a) – Hyper-parameter Tuning of KNN with GridSearchCV (Iris)¶

Goal: improve the default KNN model of Task 1(b) by searching for better hyper-parameters.

1. Parameter Grid, Cross-Validation Strategy and Search¶

  • Hyper-parameters tuned (three): n_neighbors (1–25), weights (uniform vs. distance) and the distance metric (euclidean vs. manhattan) → 25 × 2 × 2 = 100 combinations.
  • Cross-validation: stratified 5-fold on the training data only (the test set is never used for tuning).
  • Pipeline: the scaler is inside the pipeline so it is re-fitted on the training part of every fold – no information leaks from the validation fold.
  • Scoring: accuracy.
In [25]:
pipe = Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()), ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier())])

param_grid = {
    "knn__n_neighbors": list(range(1, 26)),
    "knn__weights": ["uniform", "distance"],
    "knn__metric": ["euclidean", "manhattan"],
}

cv_iris = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
grid = GridSearchCV(pipe, param_grid, cv=cv_iris, scoring="accuracy", n_jobs=1)
grid.fit(X_train, y_train)                              # raw (unscaled) training data - the pipeline scales it

print("Best parameters (best_params_):", grid.best_params_)
print(f"Best cross-validated accuracy (best_score_): {grid.best_score_:.4f}")

3. Findings and Insights¶

  • Best parameters: n_neighbors = 3, weights = 'uniform', metric = 'euclidean', with a best cross-validated accuracy of 0.9667.
  • Tuning improved the cross-validated accuracy from 0.9583 (default k = 5) to 0.9667 – one extra correctly classified flower per 120.
  • Test accuracy did not change: 0.9333 for both models. The tuned model makes exactly the same two errors (virginica predicted as versicolor). The test set has only 30 flowers, so a gain of 0.8 percentage points in cross-validation is far too small to show up there.
  • Many settings are equally good: 13 of the 100 combinations tie for the top CV accuracy, and 84 % of the settings with k between 3 and 16 reach at least 0.95 (range 0.925–0.967). Only very large k hurts – the weakest setting drops to 0.892 at k = 25 – while the whole grid spans just 0.892–0.967. On a clean, well-separated dataset like Iris, KNN is therefore fairly insensitive to hyper-parameters; tuning mainly confirms that the default was already sensible.
  • Where tuning matters more: on noisier, higher-dimensional data (such as the SMS task above) hyper-parameters change the result a lot – there GridSearchCV (and the decision threshold) gave a clear improvement.
  • Good practice followed: tuning used only the training data with 5-fold CV, the scaler sits inside the pipeline (no leakage), and the test set was used once for the final comparison.

Overall Summary¶

Task Method Key result
1(a) K-Means (Mall customers) Elbow method + silhouette → k = 5, standardised income & spending Inertia = 65.57 (scaled), silhouette 0.555; 5 clear customer segments, highest-value group = high income + high spending (39 customers)
1(b) KNN (Iris) k = 5, standardised features, 80/20 stratified split Accuracy 93.3 %, macro F1 0.933; only virginica ↔ versicolor confusion (2 errors)
1(c) Naive Bayes (SMS spam) CountVectorizer + MultinomialNB; imbalance techniques compared Baseline spam precision 0.959 / recall 0.901 → tuned model with threshold: precision 0.983, recall 0.901, F1 0.940 (ham blocked 5 → 2)
2(a) GridSearchCV (KNN, Iris) 100 combinations, stratified 5-fold CV Best: k = 3, uniform, euclidean; CV accuracy 0.9583 → 0.9667; test accuracy unchanged at 0.9333

Key lessons: (1) always scale features for distance-based algorithms (K-Means, KNN); (2) on imbalanced data judge models by the precision and recall of the minority class and choose the trade-off from the business cost of each error; (3) tune hyper-parameters with cross-validation on training data only, and be careful interpreting small differences on small test sets.
